archetypes.name: redaction-parity
archetypes.rationale: Security-critical redaction port needs a specialist to compare planned Python behavior, parity tests, and existing bash contracts for leakage or drift.
archetypes.prompt_body: Investigate whether the plan fully preserves the existing secret and path-redaction contracts while moving them into Python. Compare the proposed vectors, fail-closed PEM behavior, idempotence, and tmpdir/operator-path handling against the existing script and test surfaces named in the plan and scope. Look for missing parity cases, ambiguous replacement markers, or places where future Python logging could bypass redaction. Cite specific file paths and line ranges for any issues found, and follow the output-format rules from your outer wrapper exactly.

archetypes.name: ci-toolchain
archetypes.rationale: The plan adds a new Python toolchain and CI jobs, so config/workflow mismatches could break the phase before runtime code matters.
archetypes.prompt_body: Review the proposed CI, Makefile, and Python config plan against the repository's existing workflow conventions and lint targets. Check whether setup-python, setup-node, pip caching, command working directories, flat import resolution, and tool config file locations are mutually consistent. Pay special attention to whether the pinned dev tools and pyright Node assumption are represented in all places that will execute them. Cite specific file paths and line ranges for any issues found, and follow the output-format rules from your outer wrapper exactly.

archetypes.name: migration-boundary
archetypes.rationale: The phase promises zero live-path change while adding broad primitives, making boundary and caller-surface drift a likely plan defect.
archetypes.prompt_body: Evaluate whether the written plan actually preserves the strangler-fig boundary promised in the description. Compare the scoped files and planned updates against repo areas that could accidentally alter live /implement behavior, plugin runtime surface, hooks, or skill dispatch. Look for missing guardrails around imports, caller greps, AGENTS documentation, or CI additions that would make the new Python tree observable too early. Cite specific file paths and line ranges for any issues found, and follow the output-format rules from your outer wrapper exactly.
